items.text: Should we grant AI systems rights just in case they turn out to be conscious, even without certainty?
If AI systems are already intelligent, doesn't that make it more likely they'll become conscious as they get smarter?
Doesn't the neural-replacement thought experiment show consciousness could survive gradual replacement by silicon parts?
Couldn't a sufficiently detailed whole-brain simulation instantiate consciousness rather than just model it?
Doesn't Bostrom's simulation argument work regardless of whether computational functionalism is true?
Do the four arguments against computational functionalism depend on each other, or could one fail without undermining the rest?
Given all this admitted uncertainty about consciousness, how can Seth still insist nobody should try to build conscious AI?
Why single out organoids as the bigger worry when LLMs are the ones prompting most claims of machine consciousness?
If we rationally know an AI isn't conscious, does that resolve the ethical problem of it merely seeming conscious?
If withholding moral status has historically been a mistake with animals, why treat uncertainty about AI consciousness differently?
